Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01735
Here we can see a purely philosophical and rational position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01736
Jahm does not begin with the Qurʾanic text. He begins instead with what he believes philosophical reason requires.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01737
He bases his view of eternity on the idealist philosophical theory that movement cannot have existed without a beginning. From this he concludes that it also cannot continue without an end.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01738
He then applies the same reasoning to the world of the afterlife as he does to this world.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01739
Only after framing the problem philosophically does he return to the Qurʾanic text and interpret it according to his theory.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01740
For example, he interprets the phrase:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01741
“remaining there forever”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01742
as an expression of emphasis rather than literal endless duration.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01743
It is like saying, “May God make the rule of so-and-so everlasting.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01744
Jahm supports this interpretation with the verse:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01745
“They will remain there as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01746
He points out that this verse contains both a condition—“as long as the heavens and the earth endure”—and an exception—“except as your Lord wills.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01747
But genuine eternity, he argues, can contain neither a condition nor an exception.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01748
To apply his theory that movement can have neither an infinite past nor an infinite future consistently to Paradise, Jahm also argues that God has not yet created Paradise.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01749
The Paradise of Adam mentioned in the religious texts, he says, was created and later brought to an end.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01750
In this way, Jahm argues that Paradise is neither beginningless nor everlasting.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01751
But was Jahm really the first Muslim thinker to deny that the world of the afterlife lasts forever?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01752
There are some signs that the question had been raised before him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01753
Al-Maqdisī reports that the Companion Ibn Masʿūd said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01754
A time will come upon Hell when its doors will flap in the wind and no one will be inside, after its inhabitants have remained there for ages.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01755
He also reports that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01756
If the people of Hell remained there for as many years as there are grains of sand in ʿĀlij, they would still have something to hope for.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01757
That is, they could hope for forgiveness and eventual release from Hell.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01758
But neither statement, in our view, amounts to Jahm’s denial of an everlasting afterlife.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01759
Ibn Masʿūd and ʿUmar are speaking only about the possibility that God may eventually forgive the people being punished in Hell.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01760
Neither statement says that Paradise itself will cease to exist.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01761
According to Islamic belief, where would those released from Hell go after being forgiven?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01762
The two statements simply give sinners hope that, after receiving their share of punishment in Hell, they may eventually remain forever in Paradise.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01763
They say nothing beyond that.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01764
This is very different from Jahm’s position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01765
We can therefore say that Jahm’s view on this subject had no known precedent in Islamic thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01766
He was also unique in his own time in the philosophical reasoning he used to defend it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01766
3 — Good and Evil According to Reason
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01767
Al-Shahrastānī summarizes Jahm’s position on this question in a short phrase. While listing Jahm’s views, he writes:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01768
“...and making knowledge obligatory through reason before the arrival of revelation.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01769
What does this mean?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01770
It refers to a question that, after Jahm, became the subject of intense debate between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites, and later became one of the central issues of kalām.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01771

As Jahm first understood the problem, it meant that reason could tell what is good or bad in things and in human conduct, requiring us to do what is good and avoid what is bad. Reason can recognize all this and act on it by itself before “hearing”—that is, before people hear what the prophets and messengers bring from divine revelation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01772

Jahm may not have developed this idea systematically in the way the Muʿtazilites and later scholars of kalām would. Over time, they gave it the final philosophical form known in Muʿtazilite and kalām literature as “the question of rational good and bad.” What they meant was that reason can decide for itself what is good and what is bad before religious law arrives. Jahm’s importance lies in being the first to identify this question and give it an early theoretical form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01773

The Ashʿarites later opposed this with their own doctrine of “good and bad as determined by religious law.” They denied that good and bad exist objectively in things themselves. On their view, nothing is good or bad in itself. Something becomes good when religious law commands it, and bad when religious law forbids it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01774

At first glance, Jahm’s position may seem to have only one side, pointing in a metaphysical direction. After all, the knowledge he believes reason can reach includes knowledge of God and of principles of faith even before religion actually reveals them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01775
But we also have to see the other, rational side of the argument.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01776

First, it gives reason the power to discover the true nature of things on its own. This introduces an important new element into the theory of knowledge in Islamic thought: reason itself has an independent role in gaining knowledge.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01777
Second, it accepts that the nature of things exists objectively, independently of human awareness and understanding.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01778
In both respects, this second side has a progressive content. It also creates a real dialectical tension with the obvious idealism and metaphysics of the first side.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01778
4 — The Question of Seeing God
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01779
Most Muslims, especially the Ashʿarites, believed that God could be seen in the afterlife.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01780

They supported this with what they called a rational argument. Everything that exists, they said, can be seen. Anything that cannot possibly be seen cannot be shown to exist and is therefore as good as nonexistent. Since God’s existence has been established, it follows that seeing Him must also be possible.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01781
Their logical formula therefore rested on two claims they already accepted: first, that God exists; and second, that everything that exists can be seen.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01782
They then supported this argument with a literal, almost crudely materialist reading of Qurʾanic verses. One example was:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01783
“Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be: Peace.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01784
Al-Malaṭī explained this verse by saying that when the word “meeting” is used without qualification, it means seeing, especially when physical meeting and bodily contact are impossible.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01785
But they also went beyond this literal reading and gave some verses a metaphysical interpretation. One example was:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01786
“For those who do good is the best reward, and more. Neither darkness nor humiliation will cover their faces. These are the people of Paradise, and there they will remain forever.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01787
They said that the “best reward” was eternal life in Paradise, but that the highest pleasure in Paradise was seeing God. In other words, the joy of Paradise would not be complete without that vision.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01788
There is something important here that we should notice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01789

By this period, members of the religious schools were no longer relying only on religious texts when making their arguments. Before anything else, they were also trying to use reason and formal logic. Their arguments may look weak to us, and the logical formulas they used may have rested on metaphysical assumptions they had already accepted in advance. But the important point is that they were now trying to argue in this way at all.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01790

This was no accident. It grew out of the historical conditions of the period. Religious thinkers were becoming increasingly open to rational and logical ways of thinking, helped by their contact with the philosophical cultures of the ancient world. These methods had become intellectually necessary even for thinkers with conservative views, including those who were extremely conservative in religious matters.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01791
Jahm ibn Ṣafwān took a very different position on the question of seeing God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01792
He denied completely that God could ever be seen, either in this world or in the afterlife.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01793

His position followed from an earlier claim he had made while denying the attributes of God: that God “is not a thing.” The rule that “everything that exists can be seen” therefore did not apply to God, because an existing thing is precisely that—a “thing.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01794

Here, just as in his treatment of the divine attributes, Jahm begins from an abstract view of the reality of God. His approach comes close to philosophical thinking in concepts, even though his overall direction remains completely metaphysical.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01794
5 — The Question of God’s Knowledge
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01795

In a later period, this question became a major point of disagreement between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites. But here too, Jahm seems to have reached a position before the Muʿtazilites that they would later adopt themselves.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01796
What exactly was the disagreement?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01797

In our discussion of the Qadarites, we saw that some Qurʾanic verses appear on the surface to support predestination. They say that everything that happens in the universe and in human life happens according to a decree from God that is as eternal as God Himself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01798
This also seems to imply that God knows everything He has decreed will happen, and that His knowledge is therefore eternal as well.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01799
Some verses state this quite directly. For example:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01800
“Not a leaf falls without His knowing it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, that is not written in a clear book.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01801
Disagreement over verses like this was not limited to the question of free choice and predestination. It also produced a disagreement over God’s knowledge.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01802
Even the Jabriyya took the same position as the Muʿtazilites on this question, despite the deep difference between them over freedom and predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01803
Jahm, whom we have already seen was a leading figure of the Jabriyya, raised the question of “God’s knowledge” before the Muʿtazilites did.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01804
He argued that God’s knowledge is not eternal, despite the apparent meaning of the verses just quoted. Instead, this knowledge comes into being.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01805

Here again, Jahm goes back to the position he had already taken on the divine attributes. Knowledge is an attribute. Since he had denied attributes to God, what could he now say about God’s knowledge?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01806
Could he simply deny that God knows?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01807
He could not accept that conclusion, because denying God knowledge would mean attributing ignorance to Him. Jahm was not prepared to say that.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01808
So how did he solve the problem?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01809
Once again, he used a rational method that comes close to philosophical reasoning.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01810
Ibn Ḥazm reports Jahm as setting out the problem in these terms:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01811

“If God’s knowledge had always existed, then it must either be God Himself or something other than Him. If God’s knowledge is something other than God and has also existed eternally, then this means associating something with God”—that is, making knowledge a partner alongside God, since there would now be two eternal realities: God and His knowledge—“and giving eternity to something other than God. This is unbelief. But if God’s knowledge is God Himself, then God is knowledge”—meaning that “God” would simply mean “knowledge”—“and this is heresy.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01812
What Jahm means in the last part is that if God Himself is simply identical with knowledge, then what truly exists is knowledge, rather than God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01813
Jahm has now stated the problem in philosophical terms. But how does he solve it?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01814

He chooses a solution that denies the eternity of God’s knowledge without denying knowledge to God altogether. In other words, he says that God’s knowledge arises in time rather than existing eternally.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01815
But this immediately raises more questions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01816

How does this knowledge arise? How does God come to know something that He did not know before? Does He know a thing before it exists, or only when it comes into existence? And when this new knowledge arises, where does it exist? In what “locus,” or subject, does this newly arising knowledge of God exist?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01817
Historians of the Islamic schools give somewhat different answers to these questions, apart from the last one.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01818

The reason is that no book written by Jahm himself has survived, so we cannot read his views directly. In later centuries, his ideas and the basic principles of his doctrine became known through works describing the different Islamic schools and sects, as well as through historical and literary works from that period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01819

A number of major historians of Arab-Islamic thought discussed this particular question in their accounts of Jahm, including al-Shahrastānī, al-Ashʿarī, al-Baghdādī, al-Ṣafadī, Ibn Taymiyya, and others.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01820
Al-Shahrastānī answers the questions above by saying that Jahm accepted newly arising instances of knowledge for God that existed in no particular locus.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01821
He then reports Jahm as saying:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01822

“It is not possible for God to know a thing before creating it. For if He knew it and then created it, would His knowledge remain as it was, or would it not? If it remained as it was, it would become ignorance, because knowing that a thing will exist is different from knowing that it has already come into existence. But if His knowledge did not remain as it was, then it changed. And whatever changes is created, not eternal.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01823
After quoting this, al-Shahrastānī says that Jahm’s position agrees here with that of Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01824
He then gives the rest of Jahm’s argument:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01825

“Once it is established that knowledge comes into being, there are only two possibilities. Either God’s knowledge comes into being within His own essence, which would mean that His essence changes and that God becomes a place in which new events occur. Or it comes into being in some other locus, in which case that locus would be the thing described as possessing the knowledge, not the Creator Himself. It therefore follows that this knowledge exists in no locus.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01826
Al-Shahrastānī then says that Jahm accepted “newly arising instances of knowledge as numerous as the things known.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01827
This account gives us a fairly complete picture of how Jahm tried to solve the problem.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01828

God’s knowledge, on this view, is not eternal but arises in time. This divine knowledge exists in no locus. Nor is it one single, universal knowledge that contains everything. Instead, God has knowledge of individual things, and these instances of knowledge multiply according to the number of individual things that exist and become known to Him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01829

The question of whether God knows particulars rather than universals would later become one of the major points of disagreement between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites. Here again, Jahm anticipated a later problem in kalām.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01830
From al-Shahrastānī’s account, we can understand Jahm to mean that God cannot know a thing before that thing exists.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01831
But al-Ashʿarī reports two different views from Jahm on this part of the question.
